to a level below where it stood at the end of 2013, when its business was a fraction of its current size.
The disconnect raises an intriguing question for investors: Has Wall Street become too cautious about the AI leader?
AI Growth Shows Little Sign of Slowing

Nvidia reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion on Nov. 17, up 103% year over year and 20% sequentially. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion, increasing 110% from the year-ago period.
Net income more than doubled to $65.3 billion from $31.9 billion, while diluted earnings per share climbed 108% to $2.70.
The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The quarter includes an additional week, and the outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China.
“Our momentum is real,”
Colette Kress

, Nvidia’s interim CEO and CFO, said in the earnings release, adding that its Vera Rubin roadmap remains on track. The company also confirmed that its next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform had begun shipping.
A Valuation Reset Since 2013
data puts the chipmaker’s trailing price-to-earnings ratio at 15.68, while its forward P/E stands at 9.24. Its PEG ratio, which compares valuation with expected earnings growth, is just 0.178.

The historical comparison is particularly striking. According to CompaniesMarketCap, Nvidia ended 2013 with a P/E ratio of 19.6. Its multiple stood at 18.3 at the end of 2014 and 17.1 at the end of 2018.
The current Benzinga Pro reading is below all three historical benchmarks.
The five-year P/E chart also illustrates how sharply investor expectations have changed. Nvidia’s multiple surged above 200 in 2023 before declining through 2024, 2025 and 2026.
Note: Historical year-end figures and current valuation readings come from different data providers and may reflect differences in calculation methodology.
What Investors Should Watch

A lower P/E does not automatically make Nvidia undervalued. The multiple also reflects expectations for future earnings, which could change if AI infrastructure spending slows, competition intensifies or customers become more selective with capital investments.

Investors should watch data center growth, gross margins, customer spending and management’s forward guidance to determine whether the lower multiple represents an opportunity or a more cautious reassessment of how long the AI spending boom can last.
